payload.throughline: Define the system and sign convention first, then account for energy and entropy across thermal processes and phase changes.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: A sealed metal bottle of water cools on a bench. The analysis defines the water as the system. Which statement follows from that boundary choice? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Distinguish a system from its surroundings, separate state functions from path quantities, and apply the Zeroth Law to thermal-equilibrium relationships.

Bridge: Energy accounting begins the same way as any conservation problem: name what is inside the boundary and what may cross it. Temperature comparisons then tell whether net thermal transfer is expected.

A thermodynamic system is the matter or region selected for analysis; everything else is the surroundings. A boundary may permit energy transfer, matter transfer, both, or neither, depending on the stated model.

A state function depends only on the thermodynamic state. Internal energy and temperature are state functions. Heat and work describe energy crossing a boundary during a process, so their values can depend on the path.

The Zeroth Law states that if system A is in thermal equilibrium with B and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and C are in thermal equilibrium. Thermal equilibrium requires equal temperature and no net heat transfer between the systems.
Use three boxes: boundary, state, and path. First draw the boundary; next compare initial and final state variables; only then label heat or work transferred along the chosen path.

Two processes carry the same gas from the same initial state to the same final state. I know the internal-energy change is the same because it is a state function. I do not assume heat or work is the same because each records a path-dependent transfer.
Thermometer B equilibrates with sample A, and the same thermometer reading is obtained after B equilibrates with sample C. By the Zeroth Law, A and C have equal temperatures even if they never touch.
I rule out the claim that A and C must contain equal internal energy: equal temperature does not require equal amount, composition, or total internal energy.

Starting check: Using ΔU = q + w with w defined as work done on the system, a gas expands and pushes the surroundings. What is the sign of w? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Apply the First Law using an explicit sign convention and read pressure–volume work from rectangular areas under paths or enclosed by cycles.
Bridge: The prior KC separated endpoint changes from path transfers. Now combine them quantitatively: the internal-energy change equals the signed heat and work transfers for the chosen system.
Use the chemistry sign convention throughout this lesson: ΔU = q + w, where q is positive for heat entering the system and w is positive for work done on the system.
For expansion against a constant external pressure, w = −PextΔV. Expansion has ΔV > 0 and therefore negative work on the system; compression has positive work on the system.

On a pressure–volume diagram, the magnitude of work done by the gas is the area under the path. For rectangular segments, area is pressure times volume change, and 1 kPa·L equals 1 J. The area enclosed by a cycle gives the magnitude of net cyclic work; clockwise cycles represent net work done by the gas.

Keep a two-column energy ledger: energy entering the system is positive and energy leaving is negative. For PV work, read area first, decide expansion or compression second, then convert to work-on-system sign.

A gas absorbs 300 J and expands while doing 120 J of work on the surroundings. Under ΔU = q + w, q = +300 J and w = −120 J, so ΔU = +180 J. I do not add +120 J because that would switch conventions mid-problem.
At 100 kPa, a gas expands from 2 L to 5 L. The rectangular PV area is 100 kPa × 3 L = 300 J. That is 300 J done by the gas, so work on the gas is −300 J.
If 500 J of heat enters during this expansion, ΔU = +500 J − 300 J = +200 J.

Boundary: the sign of work cannot be inferred from the word “work” alone; identify who does work on whom. PV area gives work magnitude, while direction and the declared convention supply its sign. Calculus and curved-path integration are outside scope.

Retrieve the ledger: heat in is positive; work on the system is positive; expansion work is negative under this convention. Read PV work as area and use cycle direction to decide who performs net work.
Starting check: For the same pure substance under comparable conditions, which ordering generally has increasing entropy? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Use relative phase entropy and the Second Law to predict the allowed direction of a process from system and surroundings entropy changes.
Bridge: The First Law accounts for energy but does not by itself determine direction. Entropy accounting adds a direction test for the combined system and surroundings.

For the same substance under comparable conditions, a gas generally has greater entropy than a liquid, and a liquid greater entropy than an ordered crystal, because more microscopic arrangements are accessible.
The Second Law direction test applies to the universe: ΔSuniv = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings. A spontaneous direction has ΔSuniv > 0; equilibrium has ΔSuniv = 0.
The system’s entropy may decrease in an allowed process if the surroundings increase by a larger amount. Therefore, “system entropy always increases” is not the Second Law.
Use two entropy columns, system and surroundings, then add them. Phase ordering predicts the system sign; heat transfer or supplied data determine the surroundings sign; the sum determines direction.

Freezing makes the system more ordered, so ΔSsystem is negative. I do not stop there. If released heat raises surroundings entropy by a larger positive amount, ΔSuniv is positive and freezing is allowed in that direction.
A process has ΔSsystem = −20 J/K and ΔSsurroundings = +35 J/K. The total is +15 J/K, so the stated direction is spontaneous despite the system entropy decrease.
The reverse direction would have ΔSuniv = −15 J/K under the same conditions and would not be spontaneous.

Boundary: phase labels suggest relative system entropy, not the full direction by themselves. A gas-to-liquid change lowers system entropy, yet the process can be spontaneous when surroundings entropy increases more.

Starting check: Energy from the Sun reaches a spacecraft across nearly empty space. Which transfer mechanism carries that energy? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Use calorimetry, heat capacity, transfer mechanisms, thermal expansion, latent heat, and phase diagrams to analyze thermal changes.

Bridge: The energy ledger now becomes a thermal ledger. Separate energy that changes temperature from energy that changes phase, and identify how energy crosses from one part of the chosen system to another.
For temperature change without phase change, q = mcΔT, where c is specific heat. An object’s heat capacity is C = mc, so q = CΔT. In an isolated calorimetry model, signed heat changes sum to zero.

Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions in direct contact. Convection transfers energy with bulk fluid motion. Radiation transfers energy by electromagnetic waves and requires no material medium.

During a phase change at the transition condition, added or removed energy changes phase while temperature remains constant in the ideal model: q = mL. Heating curves therefore use sloped segments for temperature change and plateaus for phase change.

Most materials expand when temperature rises and contract when it falls. On a phase diagram, a path crossing a boundary changes phase; a point within one region does not. Read the axes and direction before naming the transition.
Use a thermal decision tree: boundary transfer mechanism → single phase or boundary crossing → q = mcΔT or q = mL → signed conservation across interacting parts.

A hot metal enters cooler water in an insulated cup. I assign the metal a negative q and the water a positive q, set their sum to zero, and use each mass and specific heat. I do not set their heat magnitudes equal without signs.
A 100 g sample with c = 2 J/(g·K) warms by 5 K. Its energy gain is q = 100 × 2 × 5 = 1000 J.
If 1000 J instead drives melting at the melting point with Lf = 50 J/g, 20 g melts while temperature remains constant. The equations represent different physical stages.
A metal lid warming in contact with hot water receives energy mainly by conduction at the interface; circulating water redistributes energy by convection, and a nearby lamp can add radiation.

Boundary: a temperature plateau during continued energy transfer need not mean “no energy change”; it can mark latent heat and changing phase fraction. Thermal expansion is a size change, not a phase change by itself.
